what: A read replica is a live, read-only copy of your database. The primary (leader) takes every write and streams the changes to its replicas (followers), which then answer read queries.
like: Like a head chef who writes each new recipe once, while photocopies go out to every counter so many people can read them at the same time.
why: Spreads read traffic over many machines so the primary has room for writes
Puts a copy in another zone or region, close to users and ready if the primary fails
Gives reports and analytics their own copy so heavy queries never slow the app

steps.d: Every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE is sent to the one primary. Having a single writer keeps the order of changes simple and clear.
The primary records each change in order in its log - the WAL (write-ahead log) in PostgreSQL, the binary log in MySQL.
Replicas pull the log and replay it. By default this is asynchronous: the primary confirms the commit without waiting, so replicas trail by a little (replication lag).
The router or app sends SELECTs to replicas and keeps writes on the primary. Reads that must see a just-made write go to the primary.
A cascading replica copies from another replica instead of the primary. That saves primary connections and cross-region bandwidth, at the cost of a bit more lag.
A monitor promotes the most caught-up replica to be the new primary and repoints traffic. With async replication the last few writes may not have arrived yet.

numbers.l: RDS read replicas per source instance, up to 5 cross-Region
Aurora Replicas per cluster, all sharing one storage volume
usual Aurora replica lag after the primary writes
typical PostgreSQL streaming lag when the standby keeps up
MySQL semisync wait before falling back to async (default)

choices.d: Async is fastest but a failover can lose recent writes. MySQL semisync waits for one replica to receive the change. PostgreSQL synchronous_commit=remote_apply waits until the standby has applied it.
PostgreSQL synchronous_standby_names can say FIRST 2 (by priority) or ANY 2 (a quorum). More acknowledgements mean safer commits but slower ones.
Send most reads to replicas, but route a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after they write, so they always see their own change.
Same zone for cheap read scaling, another zone for failover, another region for nearby users and disaster recovery. Cross-region copies add lag and transfer cost.
Automatic promotion (Aurora, RDS Multi-AZ, Patroni) or manual. Decide which replica wins, how clients find the new primary, and how other replicas follow it.

instead.why: Hot, repeated reads served from memory, cheaper than another database copy
When writes or data size outgrow one primary, split the data
Full-text and faceted search belongs in a search index
Big analytical queries over history run better in a warehouse

breaks.d: A user saves a change, the next page reads a replica that has not caught up, and the change seems missing.
breaks.see: Bug reports like 'my edit vanished, then came back'
breaks.fix: Read-your-own-writes: read from the primary for a short window after a write, or wait for the replica to reach that log position

breaks.d: Heavy write bursts or a slow replica make lag grow from milliseconds to minutes.
breaks.fix: Bigger replica, fewer large batch writes, take lagging replicas out of the read pool

breaks.d: With async replication the promoted replica may miss the newest commits.
breaks.see: Last few orders missing after a failover
breaks.fix: Semisync or a synchronous standby for data that must not be lost

breaks.d: In fully synchronous mode, commits wait for the standby, so if it disappears writes pause.
breaks.fix: Use ANY n of several standbys, or allow a timeout fallback like MySQL semisync

breaks.t: A bad change is copied too
breaks.d: An accidental DELETE replays on every replica within moments.
breaks.see: Rows missing on primary and all replicas alike
breaks.fix: Keep real backups with point-in-time restore - a replica is a copy, not a backup

say: Reads outnumber writes here, so I'll keep one primary for writes and add read replicas behind a router for the reads.
Replication is async by default, so replicas can be slightly behind - for a user's own profile right after an edit, I'll read from the primary.
One replica sits in another availability zone so we can promote it if the primary fails, and we still keep backups because replicas copy mistakes too.
If writes outgrow one primary, replicas won't help - that's when I'd look at sharding.

followups.a: Route that user's reads to the primary for a short window after a write, or record the log position (LSN) of the write and only read from a replica that has replayed past it. PostgreSQL remote_apply makes the commit wait until standbys have applied it.

Async gives the fastest writes but a failover may lose the latest commits. Sync (or semisync) waits for a replica to confirm, so it is safer but every commit pays a network round trip. Many teams run one sync standby plus async read replicas.

A monitor detects the primary is down, promotes the most up-to-date replica, and repoints the writer endpoint. Aurora can promote a reader quickly because all instances share storage. Other replicas then follow the new primary.

followups.q: Why not just add more replicas for writes?
followups.a: Every replica must replay every write, so replicas scale reads only. To scale writes you split data across primaries (sharding) or use a database built for many writers.

check.q: A user edits their bio and the next page shows the old one. Most likely cause?
check.a: The read hit a replica that had not caught up yet
d: The cache key had no TTL
check.why: Async replicas trail the primary a little. Reading your own writes from the primary fixes it.
Every replica still replays every write, so only reads spread out.

check.q: With MySQL semisync, when does the source commit?
check.a: After at least one replica confirms it received the change
check.why: Semisync waits for a receive acknowledgement, not for replicas to apply. On timeout it falls back to async.

check.q: Someone runs DELETE without a WHERE. Which saves you?
check.why: Replicas faithfully copy the mistake within moments. Only a backup lets you go back in time.
